leadership-v09-scenario-analysis-service.essentialQuestion: Can the same ten-minute outage meet a 99% time-based objective but miss a 99% request-success objective?
leadership-v09-scenario-analysis-service.verifiedBoundary: An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI over a defined period and expresses a reliability objective for the service.
leadership-v09-scenario-analysis-service.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI over a defined period and expresses a reliability objective for the service.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Read the verified claim for Service Level Objective, then analyze a hypothetical scenario. Separate observations, assumptions, the documented rule, and the conclusion. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented 24-hour ledger with 1,440 equal-duration minutes and 600,000 eligible requests. Exactly 10 whole minutes are unavailable, all 60,000 requests in those minutes fail, and every other request succeeds. Time-based and request-based SLIs count different units.

Time availability is 1,430 / 1,440, about 99.3056%, which meets the illustrative 99% objective. Request success is 540,000 / 600,000 = 90%, which misses the same numerical objective. Neither calculation overrides the other's definition.

The time-based allowance is 14.4 unavailable minutes; the request-based allowance is 6,000 failed requests. The outage uses about 69.44% of the time allowance but 1,000% of the request allowance. Converting minutes to failed requests needs traffic information, not just an availability percentage.

Move the same 10 unavailable minutes to a quiet period with only 60 failed requests while holding total requests at 600,000. Time availability is unchanged, but request success becomes 99.99% and request allowance consumption is 1%. This counterexample isolates traffic weighting.

Check equivalence only under an explicit model: if exactly the same number of requests arrives in every minute, and each minute is wholly available or unavailable, the failed-request fraction equals the unavailable-minute fraction. Partial degradation, uneven traffic and latency objectives break that shortcut.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ defines event-ratio SLIs and emphasizes choosing a user-relevant specification and measurement implementation. reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete time ledger, with a 99.9% time-based objective and a 50-minute outage on the last day of a 30-day month. There are no other unavailable minutes. Compare a completed calendar month, the next month's first complete day, and a 28-day rolling window ending after that day.

The completed month contains 43,200 minutes and permits 43.2 unavailable minutes. Its 50-minute outage misses the target; availability is about 99.8843%. Use the unrounded fraction for the pass/fail decision rather than rounding it to the displayed target.

The next calendar month's first complete day has 1,440 observed minutes and no unavailability, so month-to-date availability is 100%. That is a partial-window observation, not a guarantee of the final month's result and not evidence that the previous outage never happened.

The rolling 28-day window contains 40,320 minutes and still includes all 50 outage minutes. Its allowance is 40.32 minutes and availability is about 99.8760%, so it still misses. A calendar reset and a rolling report can disagree without either calculation being defective.

After all outage minutes eventually leave the rolling window, with no new outages, rolling availability becomes 100%. Specify interval endpoints and expire individual minutes consistently. A 31-day completed month instead permits 44.64 minutes at the same target; never assume every calendar month has 30 days.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ explains calendar-aligned versus rolling windows and why users do not forget an outage at a month boundary. The outage, minute counts and comparisons here are synthetic; four weeks is a discussed general-purpose choice, not a universal requirement.

leadership-v09-troubleshooting-lab-servi.essentialQuestion: Can two request-success ratios both display as 99.9% while only one meets an exact 99.9% objective?
leadership-v09-troubleshooting-lab-servi.verifiedBoundary: A service level objective is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI.
leadership-v09-troubleshooting-lab-servi.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A service level objective is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: A fictional team is struggling around Service Level Objective. Separate observable system facts from interpretations, identify the verified operating principle, and propose one reversible experiment. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete window with 10,000 eligible requests and a success objective of at least 99.9%. Compare two ledgers: 10 failures versus 11 failures. Counts are exact; only the displayed percentage will be rounded.

With 10 failures, 9,990 successes give exactly 99.9%, meeting the inclusive target. With 11 failures, 9,989 successes give 99.89%, missing it. Both values display as 99.9% when rounded to one decimal place.
Decide from integers: bad * 1,000 <= total. At 10 failures, 10,000 <= 10,000 is true; at 11 failures, 11,000 <= 10,000 is false. Formatting a percentage must not become the compliance algorithm.

The failed-request allowance is total / 1,000. For only 999 requests this is 0.999, so the largest compliant integer failure count is 0. At 1,000 requests exactly 1 failure is allowed; a change in sample size can change the integer boundary.

Test 9, 10 and 11 failures in the original window: the first two meet the target and the last misses. Zero eligible requests has an undefined ratio, not 100% success; define a no-data state rather than dividing by zero or inventing good events.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ defines event-ratio SLIs and SLO targets. The exact integer comparison, rounding counterexample and small-sample boundaries here are synthetic mathematical deductions, not a recommended universal traffic threshold.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented three-replica pool with fixed capacity of 1,000 requests per second per replica. Offered load is 2,700 requests per second, split as 1,500, 600 and 600. Ignore request-cost differences solely for this exercise.

Aggregate utilization is 2,700 / 3,000 = 90%, yet the first replica is at 150% of its capacity. The others are each at 60%. Spare capacity elsewhere does not automatically make the overloaded replica stable.
Redistributing 500 requests per second from the first replica, 250 to each other replica, gives 1,000, 850 and 850. Every replica is at or below modeled capacity, but the first still has no headroom.

Uniformly splitting all traffic would instead produce 900 requests per second per replica. That is mathematically feasible here, but real routing may be constrained by locality, shards, caches or state; feasibility of the totals is not proof of an available routing action.

Rejecting 500 requests per second only at the hot replica also removes its modeled overload, but sacrifices useful demand while other replicas have spare capacity. Compare the user and state-consistency consequences rather than declaring one response universally correct.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ notes that load-balancing problems and partitions can create pockets of overload despite capacity planning. This allocation exercise is synthetic, with equal-cost requests and interchangeable replicas explicitly assumed.

leadership-v10-field-note-cascading-fail.verifiedBoundary: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.
leadership-v10-field-note-cascading-fail.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented one-minute model with 400 original backend attempts and a backend allowance of 550 total attempts. Each of 4 client processes may issue up to 25 extra retries per minute; budgets are independent and all are consumed in the worst case.

The four processes permit 100 retries in total, so the upper bound is 500 attempts. Doubling to 8 client processes while keeping the same original demand permits 200 retries and raises the bound to 600, exceeding the allowance.

The global retry allowance compatible with the stated backend limit is 550 - 400 = 150. If 8 equal independent budgets must use whole retry tokens, each can receive at most 18: total retries are 144 and total attempts 544, leaving 6 unused tokens.

A genuinely shared 150-retry budget could use those remaining tokens, but requires correct scope and coordination. Eight separate copies labeled global would permit 1,200 retries instead; a label does not create shared enforcement.

These are budget ceilings, not expected traffic. Bursts within the minute and additional callers can still overload a backend whose per-second capacity is lower. A field note should record scope, interval, original traffic assumptions and the number of active budget holders.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ discusses process-wide retry budgets and considering retry behavior across the service. The scaling example and integer allocations are synthetic deductions.

leadership-v10-explain-back-challenge-ca.verifiedBoundary: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented discrete one-second model: original arrivals are always 1,050, capacity is 1,000 attempts per interval, and every rejected attempt retries exactly once in the next interval. There is no per-request cap in this deliberately unsafe model, no queue and no early success beyond the admitted capacity.
Let R(n) be retries arriving in interval n, starting R(0) = 0. Rejected work is 1,050 + R(n) - 1,000, so R(n+1) = R(n) + 50. Original demand stays fixed while retry demand grows.
The first five retry counts are 0, 50, 100, 150 and 200; offered attempts are 1,050, 1,100, 1,150, 1,200 and 1,250. Rejections in those intervals total 50 + 100 + 150 + 200 + 250 = 750.

The 750 rejected attempts are not necessarily 750 distinct failed user operations, because the same operation may be retried repeatedly. A count of attempts cannot by itself establish the user-failure count.

An enforced aggregate cap of 100 retries per interval would bound offered work at 1,150 under these assumptions, but still leave excess above capacity. A retry cap limits amplification; it does not fix the original 50-request overload or guarantee fair admission.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ describes retry amplification as positive feedback and warns against interpreting retry volume as only a symptom. This recurrence is an original synthetic model with its unsafe assumptions made explicit.

leadership-v10-decision-brief-error-budg.essentialQuestion: How does an explicit error-budget policy distinguish a missed SLO from a single incident that warrants a postmortem?
leadership-v10-decision-brief-error-budg.verifiedBoundary: An error budget is the amount of unreliability permitted by an SLO and can be used to balance reliability work with change velocity.
leadership-v10-decision-brief-error-budg.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: This invented decision brief adopts, for exercise purposes only, the example policy in the SRE Workbook: a preceding four-week SLO miss halts ordinary releases, with stated P0/security exceptions; a single incident consuming more than 20% of the budget requires a postmortem. These are chosen policy rules, not laws of reliability.

For 2,000,000 valid requests and a 99.9% objective, the window allows 2,000 failures. If 1,600 have occurred, 400 remain and 80% is consumed. The window has not missed its objective, although the remaining budget is limited.

A single incident with 450 failures consumes 450 / 2,000 = 22.5% of the window's budget. It crosses the more-than-20% postmortem boundary even though total failures are still only 1,600. The incident count is a subset of the total, not 450 additional errors.

Do not compare the incident with the remaining 400 failures: 450 / 400 = 112.5% uses the wrong denominator for this policy. Also, satisfying an SLO does not automatically approve a release; ordinary release controls still apply.

Change only total window failures to 2,100. The balance becomes -100 and success is 99.895%, below 99.9%, so ordinary releases stop under the adopted policy. For the incident trigger, exactly 400 failures is 20% and does not satisfy the strict more-than rule; 401 does.

Source and limits: https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/ is an example policy with explicit exception and escalation provisions. The invented counts exercise its distinctions; they do not authorize actual releases, prescribe another organization's policy or establish a contractual SLA.

leadership-v10-checklist-lab-error-budge.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

reasoningSteps: Take an invented window containing 100,000 valid user requests with 120 failures, plus 20,000 always-successful synthetic probes. The declared 99.9% SLO is for user requests; probes are excluded from both numerator and denominator.
The valid-user budget is 100 failures. Actual user success is 99,880 / 100,000 = 99.88%, so the balance is -20 and the SLO is missed.

If a dashboard incorrectly adds probes, it reports 119,880 / 120,000 = 99.9%, exactly meeting the target. The apparent improvement comes from changing the population, not from repairing one user request.

An independent failure-count check gives 1 - 120 / 100,000 = 0.9988. Against the polluted denominator it becomes 1 - 120 / 120,000 = 0.999. The 20,000 probes also inflate the computed allowance from 100 to 120.

Change only probe count to 100,000. The false aggregate becomes 199,880 / 200,000 = 99.94% while valid-user success remains 99.88%. Removing probes from the numerator alone is also wrong; exclusions must apply consistently to both counts.

Sources and limits: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ treats SLI definitions as the basis of reliability decisions, and https://sre.google/workbook/error-budget-policy/ explicitly discusses out-of-scope users and miscategorized errors. The event labels and counts here are invented. An exclusion needs a documented user-relevant definition, not a convenient way to hide failures.

leadership-v10-diagnostic-lab-error-budg.essentialQuestion: Why can one failure produce an enormous burn rate on a quiet service without proving that an immediate page is the right response?

leadership-v10-diagnostic-lab-error-budg.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Invent one symptom related to Error Budget. Write three competing hypotheses and one observation that can eliminate each hypothesis. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented low-traffic service with a 99.9% request-success objective. In one five-minute observation it receives 20 valid requests and one fails. This is an observed count ratio, not a reliable estimate of a stationary long-run failure probability.

The observed error fraction is 1 / 20 = 5%, giving burn 0.05 / 0.001 = 50. A zero-failure five-minute observation would report burn 0. The difference of one event therefore changes the apparent burn dramatically.

Suppose the complete 30-day window contains 10,000 valid requests and 3 failures. Its allowance is 10 and its observed consumption is 30%, leaving 7. The five-minute failure is already one of those three; do not add it twice.

Multiplying the short-window burn by time assumes a representative traffic and error process. At a constant burn of 50, a hypothetical unused 30-day budget would last 30 / 50 = 0.6 days, or 14.4 hours. That conditional projection is not a forecast from these sparse, unevenly distributed requests.

Change only the short-window denominator to 200 while retaining one failure. Its burn falls to 5. This does not establish lower severity for that failed user's transaction. Operational urgency also depends on user impact, sustained evidence and the alert policy, not only on the ratio.

Source and limits: https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/ discusses low-traffic services and the trade-offs among detection, precision and response. These invented event totals do not set a production paging threshold, justify ignoring a failed transaction or prove recovery after a zero-error sample.

leadership-v10-worked-walkthrough-gracef.essentialQuestion: How many full-quality requests can a fixed CPU budget support while still serving the rest in a cheaper degraded mode?
leadership-v10-worked-walkthrough-gracef.verifiedBoundary: Graceful degradation preserves a reduced but useful level of service when dependencies or capacity are impaired instead of failing every feature together.
leadership-v10-worked-walkthrough-gracef.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Graceful degradation preserves a reduced but useful level of service when dependencies or capacity are impaired instead of failing every feature together.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Work through a small Graceful Degradation example. Mark each reasoning step and identify exactly which step depends on the verified claim. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented one-second CPU-work budget of 8,000 CPU-ms, equivalent to 8 fully utilized cores in this simplified model. Demand is 1,000 requests per second; a full response costs 12 CPU-ms and a degraded response costs 4 CPU-ms. Ignore scheduling overhead and other bottlenecks.

Serving every request at full quality requires 12,000 CPU-ms per second, or 150% of budget. Serving every request in degraded mode requires 4,000 CPU-ms per second, or 50%. A cheaper response reduces work; it does not create CPU capacity.
If x requests use full quality, total work is 12x + 4(1,000 - x) = 4,000 + 8x. Staying within 8,000 requires x <= 500. At 500 full and 500 degraded responses the model uses the entire budget.

A mix of 400 full and 600 degraded responses costs 7,200 CPU-ms, or 90% of budget. At 501 full responses, cost is 8,008 CPU-ms and exceeds the bound. These figures omit reserves for bursts and are not production utilization recommendations.

Degraded mode must preserve essential correctness and clearly defined user expectations. Decide which requests are eligible using an explicit policy, and test the seldom-used path; silently returning incorrect results is not graceful degradation. CPU feasibility alone does not establish latency or fairness.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ defines graceful degradation as reducing work by returning lower-quality results and emphasizes testing rarely exercised paths. The cost model, mix and bounds are original synthetic calculations.

leadership-v10-reasoning-check-latency-d.verifiedBoundary: Service latency should be considered as a distribution because averages can hide slow-tail behavior experienced by some requests.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented first sample of 20 requests: 19 take 10 ms and 1 takes 300 ms. Define nearest-rank p99 as the sorted value at ceil(0.99 * n); this is a sample statistic, not a population guarantee.
For 20 requests, the rank is 20, so sample p99 equals 300 ms. The slow request is 1 / 20 = 5% of this small sample.

Append 80 new requests at 10 ms. Now there are 100 requests, 99 fast and the same one slow. The p99 rank is 99 and its value is 10 ms; the original 300 ms event is unchanged and is now 1% of the sample.

The mean also changes, from 24.5 ms to 12.9 ms, because the expanded population includes many fast requests. Neither change proves that the old outlier was repaired, and the two summaries cover different observation counts.

Do not infer a reliable population p99 or a trend from these two constructed samples alone. Sampling method, workload mix, window definition and uncertainty need separate evidence; this exercise demonstrates an arithmetic boundary, not statistical confidence.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ encourages examining latency distributions and choosing suitable measurement resolution. The sample-size counterexample and percentile convention are synthetic deductions.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented sorted sample of ten latencies: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 ms. Compare two explicitly defined sample-quantile conventions rather than assuming all tools implement the same one.

Nearest-rank p95 uses ceil(0.95 * 10) = 10, returning 100 ms. A linear convention using one-based position 1 + (n - 1) * p gives 9.55, then interpolates 55% of the way from 90 to 100 ms, returning 95.5 ms.
Both values follow their stated definitions. The disagreement alone does not prove bad input data or an implementation error. At p90 the same conventions return 90 ms and 91 ms respectively.

For a strict event rule below 95 ms, exactly 9 of 10 observations qualify, or 90%. Count events directly for such a rule; do not silently replace a target event fraction with an undocumented interpolated percentile comparison.

Specify convention, interpolation, ties, empty-sample behavior, window and population when comparing tools. This example defines the linear formula itself; it does not assert that any named product uses it.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ argues for looking at distributions and meaningful monitoring summaries. The two quantile definitions and arithmetic comparison here are original synthetic mathematics, not methods prescribed by that chapter.

leadership-v10-flash-review-saturation-s.essentialQuestion: How many active requests fit in an 8 GiB memory budget when fixed use, per-request use and a reserve are all counted?
leadership-v10-flash-review-saturation-s.verifiedBoundary: In SRE monitoring, saturation describes how full or constrained a service resource is, often indicating proximity to capacity limits.
leadership-v10-flash-review-saturation-s.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: In SRE monitoring, saturation describes how full or constrained a service resource is, often indicating proximity to capacity limits.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Summarize Saturation Signal in no more than three lines, then compare it with the verified claim and remove anything the evidence does not support. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented memory model with an 8 GiB total limit, 2 GiB fixed use and exactly 12 MiB retained per active request. Use binary units: 1 GiB = 1,024 MiB. The model omits allocator overhead and shared pages.
The total limit is 8,192 MiB and fixed use is 2,048 MiB, leaving 6,144 MiB. With no reserve, 6,144 / 12 = 512 active requests exactly exhaust the modeled remainder.
With an additional 1 GiB reserve, request state may use at most 5,120 MiB. The largest integer count is 426, because 426 * 12 = 5,112 MiB; 427 would require 5,124 MiB.

At 426 requests, modeled actual use excluding the reserve is 7,160 MiB, leaving 1,032 MiB free. At 427 requests, adding fixed use, request use and the reserve totals 8,196 MiB, exceeding the limit by 4 MiB.

These are bookkeeping ceilings, not safe real concurrency settings. Unequal request sizes, caches, allocator fragmentation and temporary allocations can invalidate a constant-per-request assumption. A chosen reserve must be justified rather than copied from the example.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ frames saturation around constrained resources such as memory. This binary-unit budget and reserve are synthetic teaching fixtures, not a claim about actual process memory.

leadership-v10-prediction-lab-saturation.essentialQuestion: How should a time-to-full estimate change when a disk reserve and a temporary compaction allocation are included?
leadership-v10-prediction-lab-saturation.verifiedBoundary: In SRE monitoring, saturation describes how full or constrained a service resource is, often indicating proximity to capacity limits.
leadership-v10-prediction-lab-saturation.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: In SRE monitoring, saturation describes how full or constrained a service resource is, often indicating proximity to capacity limits.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Before opening the evidence, predict the outcome of a small Saturation Signal scenario. Then reveal the verified claim and explain any mismatch. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented disk model with 250 GiB capacity, 210 GiB currently used and constant net growth of 2 GiB per hour. Net growth already includes ordinary writes and deletions; the linear rate is an assumption, not a forecast guarantee.
The raw free space is 40 GiB, giving 20 hours to the nominal full point. If operations require a 10 GiB reserve, usable growth headroom is only 30 GiB, giving 15 hours to that guardrail.

If a compaction task immediately adds 20 GiB of temporary data while the original data remains allocated, used space becomes 230 GiB. Raw time to full falls to 10 hours and time to the 10 GiB reserve threshold falls to 5 hours at the same net growth rate.

When temporary data is later reclaimed, the projection must be recomputed from the new state. Do not assume cleanup happens before the guardrail unless its timing is established; temporary and permanent usage must not be double-counted.

If net growth doubles to 4 GiB per hour before compaction, the original reserve horizon becomes 7.5 hours. If net growth is zero or negative, this constant-rate model predicts no future fill event; it does not justify reporting an infinite safety guarantee against bursts or other changes.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/ includes predicting impending disk saturation and choosing measurement resolution. Capacity, reserve, compaction size and rates here are synthetic, with no real storage operation authorized.

leadership-v10-recovery-lab-service-leve.essentialQuestion: After an incident ends, why can the full-window success ratio remain below target while recent requests all succeed?
leadership-v10-recovery-lab-service-leve.verifiedBoundary: An SLI is a quantitative measure of a defined aspect of service behavior, such as successful request ratio or latency.
leadership-v10-recovery-lab-service-leve.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: An SLI is a quantitative measure of a defined aspect of service behavior, such as successful request ratio or latency.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Design a recovery drill involving Service Level Indicator. Define the starting state, failure condition, expected recovery evidence, and stop/rollback criteria. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete ledger: the first 1,000 requests include 100 failures, followed by 9,000 successful requests after recovery. The full window and the post-recovery interval answer different questions; neither contains missing telemetry in this exercise.

The full window has 9,900 successes out of 10,000 requests, or 99%. The post-recovery interval is 100% successful. Recent recovery does not delete the 100 historical failures from the full-window numerator or denominator.

For an illustrative full-window 99.9% target, with no new failures, total requests must reach 100,000 because 100 * 1,000 <= total. Starting from 10,000 requests, this requires another 90,000 successes, not another repair action.

Check one request below the boundary: 100 failures among 99,999 requests still miss the exact target, even if a rounded display looks compliant. At 100,000 requests the target is met exactly. This assumes the original failures remain inside the reporting window.

A rolling-window report may instead improve as old failures expire; a calendar report may reset. Do not infer which happened from the ratio alone. Track request counts, window endpoints and event timestamps before attributing a change to recovery.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ explains event-ratio SLIs and reporting windows. The ledger and dilution boundary are synthetic deductions, not an instruction to generate artificial traffic or hide an incident.

leadership-v10-concept-mapping-lab-servi.essentialQuestion: Does multiplying 98% coverage, 99% conditional correctness and 98% conditional freshness determine how many expected pipeline records are both correct and fresh?
leadership-v10-concept-mapping-lab-servi.verifiedBoundary: A service level indicator is a quantitative measure of some aspect of service level, such as availability, latency, or error rate.
leadership-v10-concept-mapping-lab-servi.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A service level indicator is a quantitative measure of some aspect of service level, such as availability, latency, or error rate.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Draw a concept map with Service Level Indicator in the center. Link prerequisites, consequences, adjacent concepts, and the authoritative evidence; label relationship verbs. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete batch of 10,000 expected unique records. The pipeline produces 9,800 records; 98 produced records are incorrect, 196 are stale, and 49 are both. Freshness means record age below a declared threshold; all counts use the same batch and unique record identity.

Coverage is 9,800 / 10,000 = 98%. Conditional correctness among produced records is 9,702 / 9,800 = 99%, and conditional freshness is 9,604 / 9,800 = 98%. These conditional ratios exclude missing records; label that exclusion.

Among produced records, the union of incorrect or stale records has 98 + 196 - 49 = 245 members. Thus 9,555 produced records are both correct and fresh, and their fraction of all expected records is 95.55%. The overlap must be known before multiplying conditional ratios is justified.

Reconcile by disjoint categories: 200 missing, 49 incorrect-and-stale, 49 incorrect-only, 147 stale-only and 9,555 correct-and-fresh. Their sum is 10,000. Multiplying 98% coverage, 99% conditional correctness and 98% conditional freshness gives 95.0796%, which wrongly assumes independence of the last two conditions.

If the expected-record inventory omits 500 truly expected records, the measured denominator is not trustworthy. The source warns that coverage metrics can miss records a pipeline does not know about; a clean ratio cannot prove the inventory is complete.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ discusses pipeline freshness, coverage and correctness, including unknown expected records and representative correctness checks. All counts and the intentional wrong answer are synthetic.

leadership-v10-fault-isolation-lab-servi.essentialQuestion: Why can duplicated failure logs make an otherwise complete request-success metric look worse than the unique-request ledger?
leadership-v10-fault-isolation-lab-servi.verifiedBoundary: A service level indicator is a quantitative measure of some aspect of service level, such as availability, latency, or error rate.
leadership-v10-fault-isolation-lab-servi.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A service level indicator is a quantitative measure of some aspect of service level, such as availability, latency, or error rate.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Construct a fictional failure around Service Level Indicator. Narrow it from broad layer/category to one testable cause without changing multiple variables at once. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented ledger of 1,000 eligible unique requests: 980 succeed and 20 fail. A logging retry emits a second copy of each failed event, so storage contains 1,020 rows. Assume a reliable request identifier and no legitimate multiple events per request in this model.

The unique-request success ratio is 980 / 1,000 = 98%. Counting raw log rows gives 980 / 1,020, about 96.0784%. The apparent regression comes from observation duplication, not additional user failures.

Deduplicate by the specified request identity, retaining exactly one equivalent outcome per request. The denominator returns to 1,000 and the bad count to 20. Deduplicating only the bad numerator while leaving 1,020 in the denominator would instead report about 98.0392%, another inconsistent result.

Now add 10 duplicated success rows as well. Raw rows become 1,030 and raw successes 990, giving about 96.1165%; unique outcomes remain unchanged at 98%. A row-count metric can move even when user outcomes do not.

If two rows with the same identifier disagree on success, the assumed equivalent-copy model no longer holds. Flag the conflict for investigation instead of choosing the favorable outcome. Retries with distinct attempt identities require a different unit-of-counting policy.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ distinguishes the desired SLI specification from its measurement implementation and coverage limitations. The duplicate-log model is an original synthetic instrumentation counterexample, not a claim about a particular logging product.

leadership-v10-transfer-challenge-servic.essentialQuestion: Can a service meet its typical-latency objective while failing its long-tail objective, even when the mean looks acceptable?
leadership-v10-transfer-challenge-servic.verifiedBoundary: An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI over a defined period and expresses a reliability objective for the service.
leadership-v10-transfer-challenge-servic.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: An SLO is a target value or range for an SLI over a defined period and expresses a reliability objective for the service.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Apply the verified rule for Service Level Objective to a new hypothetical context. Identify which parts transfer directly and which require new evidence. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented ledger of 10,000 successful requests: 9,000 complete at 50 ms, 900 at 500 ms and 100 at 5,000 ms. Illustrative objectives require at least 90% below 100 ms and at least 99.5% below 1,000 ms. All thresholds are strict.

The fast group contains 9,000 requests, so 90% meet the 100 ms threshold and the first objective passes exactly. The two faster groups total 9,900 requests, so only 99% meet the 1,000 ms threshold and the second objective fails.

The arithmetic mean is (9,000 * 50 + 900 * 500 + 100 * 5,000) / 10,000 = 140 ms. That single mean does not show that 100 users waited 5 seconds; comparing the mean with an event-ratio threshold would test the wrong metric.

The long-tail objective permits at most 50 requests at or above 1,000 ms. Moving exactly 50 of the 5,000 ms requests to 500 ms yields 9,950 qualifying requests and exactly 99.5%, meeting it; moving only 49 leaves 9,949 and 99.49%, still failing.

Verify threshold nesting: every request below 100 ms must also be below 1,000 ms, but the reverse need not hold. A request at exactly 1,000 ms is outside the long-tail good set. Successful transport is held constant here; failure or correctness objectives require additional evidence.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ recommends multiple latency grades to represent typical experience and the long tail. The three-bucket ledger, 90% and 99.5% targets and arithmetic are invented teaching choices, not universal service requirements.

leadership-v10-scenario-brief-service-le.essentialQuestion: Can an aggregate 99.9% success objective pass while one critical user task fails for one in ten requests?
leadership-v10-scenario-brief-service-le.verifiedBoundary: A service level objective is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI.
leadership-v10-scenario-brief-service-le.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A service level objective is a target value or range for a service level measured by an SLI.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Analyze a hypothetical Service Level Objective scenario using four headings: observations, assumptions, verified rule, conclusion. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete service ledger with two disjoint tasks: browsing receives 999,000 requests with 400 failures, and checkout receives 1,000 requests with 100 failures. Every eligible request belongs to exactly one task; the task names are illustrative.

Overall there are 1,000,000 requests and 500 failures, so success is 99.95% and a 99.9% aggregate objective passes. Checkout succeeds on 900 / 1,000 requests, or 90%; aggregate compliance does not imply every task meets the same target.

The aggregate allowance is 1,000 failures, leaving 500. A separately adopted 99.9% checkout objective would allow only 1 failure, so its 100 failures consume 10,000% of that allowance. This separate objective is a proposed teaching scenario, not an already approved business commitment.

Add 1,000,000 successful browsing requests without changing checkout. Aggregate success rises to 99.975%, while checkout remains at 90%. More low-risk traffic can hide a critical-task problem in the aggregate without repairing it.

Do not conclude all routes require identical targets or that every checkout failure has identical business impact. Identify critical user journeys with evidence, then choose scope, thresholds and ownership before evaluating compliance. Avoid inventing targets after observing which ones pass.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ recommends considering common tasks and critical activities and using critical user journeys to improve coverage of customer experience. The traffic split and targets here are synthetic.

leadership-v10-exam-style-practice-servi.essentialQuestion: If 99% of requests succeed and 99% are fast, what can you prove about the percentage that are both successful and fast?

reasoningSteps: Use an invented complete population of 10,000 requests with 100 failures and 100 slow requests. The overlap is not supplied. Success and fast must both hold for the proposed joint objective; the two marginal ratios alone do not identify that joint ratio.

At one extreme the failed and slow sets are disjoint: 200 requests violate at least one condition, leaving 9,800 jointly good, or 98%. At the other extreme the two bad sets coincide: only 100 requests are bad, leaving 9,900 jointly good, or 99%.

Therefore the joint good percentage is bounded from 98% to 99%. Multiplying the marginal ratios gives 98.01%, which is one possible result under an independence assumption, not a result established by the two counts alone.

An inclusive 98.5% joint objective requires no more than 150 bad requests. Since bad union = 200 - overlap, it passes exactly when the bad-set overlap is at least 50. Overlap 49 gives 9,849 jointly good and 98.49%, while overlap 50 gives 9,850 and 98.5%.

The labels success and fast must use the same eligible requests, observation window and threshold definition. If one metric excludes failures or uses another window, even these bounds cannot be applied to the two reported percentages without reconciling populations.

Source review: https://sre.google/workbook/implementing-slos/ explains event-ratio specifications and successful calls below latency thresholds. The set bounds and threshold proof are original synthetic mathematics; independence is not asserted by the source.

leadership-v10-measurement-lab-cascading.essentialQuestion: Can high backend attempt throughput conceal low useful user throughput during a retry storm?
leadership-v10-measurement-lab-cascading.verifiedBoundary: A cascading failure occurs when a failure or overload in one component increases stress on other components and propagates through the system.
leadership-v10-measurement-lab-cascading.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A cascading failure occurs when a failure or overload in one component increases stress on other components and propagates through the system.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Define what you would measure to evaluate a Cascading Failure hypothesis. Separate the measurement from the conclusion and state what result would change your mind. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented ten-second ledger of 1,000 user operations and 2,500 backend attempts. Exactly 800 operations finish successfully within their deadlines; 200 do not. Of the attempts, 1,500 fail, 800 provide those timely completions and 200 return successful but duplicate or too-late results.

Backend attempt throughput is 250 attempts per second, while useful timely operation throughput is only 80 operations per second. The attempt-success ratio is 1,000 / 2,500 = 40%; timely operation completion is 800 / 1,000 = 80%. Different populations must stay labeled.

The attempt amplification is 2.5 attempts per original operation. Only 800 / 2,500 = 32% of attempts yield a distinct timely completion in this fixture; the remaining 68% do not. This classification requires operation identifiers and deadline evidence, not merely HTTP success codes.

Now compare a second synthetic policy using 1,200 attempts to achieve the same 800 timely completions for the same 1,000 operations. Attempt throughput drops to 120 per second while useful throughput stays 80. Lower raw throughput can therefore accompany less wasted work rather than worse user service.

Do not infer that every repeated attempt is waste in every system: a retry may be the one that succeeds, and side effects may need reconciliation. The ledger explicitly labels outcomes; without that evidence, aggregate counts cannot identify which attempt was useful.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ describes retries and expired work consuming resources without useful progress. The two policy ledgers are synthetic comparisons, not measured performance or a proof that a particular retry configuration is optimal.

leadership-v10-transfer-lab-cascading-fa.essentialQuestion: How much unnecessary work can cancellation propagation prevent after a critical parallel branch fails?
leadership-v10-transfer-lab-cascading-fa.verifiedBoundary: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.
leadership-v10-transfer-lab-cascading-fa.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Apply the verified rule for Cascading Failure to a new hypothetical context. Identify which parts transfer directly and which require new evidence. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented parallel-call model with three children starting together and each consuming one CPU-ms per wall-clock ms while active. Critical child A fails at 20 ms; children B and C would each run for 200 ms, but their results are useless once A has failed.
Without propagated cancellation, total child work is 20 + 200 + 200 = 420 CPU-ms. The logical operation has already become unsuccessful at 20 ms, yet the other work continues.
If cancellation reaches B and C 10 ms after A fails and they stop immediately, each runs for 30 ms. Total child work becomes 20 + 30 + 30 = 80 CPU-ms, saving 340 CPU-ms.

Cancellation does not undo completed side effects or prove that no deeper work remains. If each child has spawned descendants, cancellation must reach those descendants or their work continues. The calculation assumes no cancellation overhead beyond the stated delay.

If B or C is performing an essential checkpoint or an irreversible action, abrupt interruption may be unsafe. Define safe stopping points and reconciliation rules rather than treating cancellation as transactional rollback.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ describes cancellation propagation through RPC trees and circumstances where safe completion/checkpointing matters. The child timings and CPU model are synthetic and exclude network and scheduling costs.

vocabulary.term: Incident Leadership: Create Clarity Under Pressure
vocabulary.definition: During a major incident, leadership is the work of establishing roles, priorities, communication, and decision cadence so technical responders can solve the problem.

vocabulary.term: Delegation: Transfer Outcomes, Not Just Tasks
vocabulary.definition: Effective delegation gives someone a clear outcome, authority boundaries, context, resources, and a feedback loop.

vocabulary.term: Error Budgets: Reliability Has a Cost
vocabulary.definition: An error budget converts an availability or reliability objective into an explicit allowance for imperfect service over a measurement window.
Google SRE argues that 100% reliability is usually the wrong target because achieving the final increments of reliability can impose disproportionate cost and restrict change.
Setting an SLO requires choosing a target that reflects user needs and business constraints rather than assuming maximum possible availability is always optimal.
Reliability objectives are most useful when they describe observable service behavior that matters to users, not internal component health alone.

leadership-v10-configuration-lab-cascadi.essentialQuestion: How many retry attempts fit inside a fixed deadline when backoff delays and attempt execution both consume time?
leadership-v10-configuration-lab-cascadi.verifiedBoundary: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.
leadership-v10-configuration-lab-cascadi.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a control room where people need roles, signals, priorities, communication, and feedback. Real organizations vary; use the analogy only to organize the lesson.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: A cascading failure occurs when failure or overload in one component increases pressure on other components, causing additional failures.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use a fictional team/service and separate observations, assumptions, decisions, owners, and measurable outcomes. Create a reversible lab configuration around Cascading Failure. Predict the result, record the change, observe the result, then revert it. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: This topic is version-sensitive. Check current vendor, project, or standards documentation before operational use.

reasoningSteps: Use an invented deterministic schedule for one operation with an absolute 500 ms deadline. Each attempt takes 80 ms; waits after successive failures are 50, 100 and 200 ms. This fixed schedule is a calculation fixture, not a recommendation to omit jitter.
The first attempt runs from 0 to 80 ms. After waiting 50 ms, the second runs from 130 to 210 ms. After waiting 100 ms, the third runs from 310 to 390 ms. Three complete attempts fit.

The next 200 ms wait would place the fourth start at 590 ms, already past the deadline; its nominal finish would be 670 ms. A count-only limit of four attempts must not authorize that fourth call after expiration.

Reducing the deadline to 350 ms leaves only two complete 80 ms attempts in this fixture; the third would finish at 390 ms. Starting a call with too little remaining budget may still be allowed by a real API that can finish sooner or cancel, so distinguish this fixed-duration feasibility model from an implementation policy.

Multiple clients following identical deterministic waits can synchronize. Randomized backoff spreads attempt times but does not eliminate limits, deadlines or worst-case capacity concerns. Test randomness with controlled seeds separately from this deterministic arithmetic.

Source review: https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/ recommends randomized exponential backoff, bounded retries and propagated deadlines. The timings here are original synthetic values and do not prescribe a real retry policy.
